original_text: NTA I am always amazed at the shame people accept as punishment for "snooping" on their children's electronics, when their intuition or their childs actions prompt them to do so....And they find incriminating evidence of wrong doing. There is no shame in protecting their self-worth, self-respect, your families emotional well-being and the obvious boundaries in any family relationship not to mention the need to discover when a child is headed down a dark path or is showing hidden mental instability....nobody else will do it for you...and obviously you have discovered your child cannot be trusted to hold steady. It happens all the time. In my household we have an open electronics policy. That is the true test of trust. There is nothing I don't know about my entire families social media, and the same goes for me. It's the only way to be. If your loved ones won't let you go thru their phone or their computer then they are hiding something from you. Totally unacceptable in today's predatory world where the most egregious of horrors can invade your inner sanctum via the internet, twisting young minds. I have been where you are. My child was selling heroin via his computer and phone to the neighborhood kids. I thought he was just popular. He was 13 years old. I found his stash of money under his bed one day. A shit load of bucks. I knew it wasn't from mowing grass, so I went thru his computer. Figured it out pretty quick. If I didn't put the hammer down, and put it down hard...my son would have ended up living a life of crime, in jail or worse. I didn't smash his electronics, I completely removed all electronics from our home. I was the only person who had a phone. He went back to the stone age. He hated my guts, made our lives miserable for a few years. But with therapy, new friends, lots of extracurricular activities, a tutor, and patience..God the patience...he has become a person to be proud of. And yes, he eventually earned the PRIVILEGED of using a computer and having a phone again. As a father, you must stand your ground. You cannot change his thought process, it is learned from his internet use and the people he associates with. He needs intensive therapy (yes, I would suggest a male), new and a better quality of friends, more involvement from you as a role model...and no access to any electronics without your ass being right next to him. And no, he does not NEED a phone. No gaming either. Discover your neighborhood library instead. Good Luck! ​ ​

original_text: I can’t say either way. There’s probably poor actions on both sides of this, but it’s such a delicate subject, so... Terminating a pregnancy affects women and men differently, and neither one can really put themselves in the other person’s shoes here. It’s a highly emotional situation, but still needed to be discussed rationally - which doesn’t appear to have been the case, so I’m not surprised it blew up. While his feelings do matter, he should of been more supportive and (both of you) should have waited for things to cool down before making a final decision on your relationship - you both went through a major trauma, with you having to shoulder the hardest part. Your fluctuating emotional state should have been taken into account. Highly emotional situations are a breeding ground for volatile outcomes, and issuing demands/ultimatums when everyone’s mental state is being severely stressed is never a good idea. Ultimatums should be a last-ditch effort, used only after all other options are exhausted, and have been thought through very carefully. You also have to be prepared for the person to make the less desirable option when given one as well.

original_text: NTA. I would have been so proud of you. You did nothing wrong and you shouldn't feel reluctant to go to other meet-ups. But perhaps you could join some groups centered around your own interests and go without her. The nice thing about meeting strangers is that they don't know you're supposed to be "a social Neanderthal" and you can try on a more social self when around them. Also, based on your account here, it doesn't sound like you don't understand social etiquette. I wonder how you developed some of these ideas: has someone told you repeatedly you're socially inadequate? were you always around idiots who thought making small talk was the epitome of socialization? have you ever had a friend with whom you could talk for hours? I used to think I was charmless and introverted because I'd never enjoyed large gatherings and the sort of pointless chatter which dominates them. Now I can do it easily if necessary, but it bores me to death. However, at some point, I realized I was very good at talking to people one-on-one, including those who didn't normally communicate much, and that I could keep a conversation going with anyone. I still think of myself as being closer to the introverted end of the spectrum, but I don't see it as a bad thing: I choose my social encounters carefully and don't waste energy on those I know I don't personally enjoy. I'll be honest: I don't like your girlfriend's reaction. I don't like the fact that maybe she uses you to feel good about herself and that she resented you for having a successful evening.
